cells.tense: Several feelings are still possible and you're the one holding them open.
cells.ask: Name the one you actually want to follow, then take one plain step toward it today — the small one that doesn't require anyone's answer first.
cells.core:
You can hold a few possible feelings at once without being ruled by them. Someone says a thing and you feel the pull of what they might mean, and you let it stay a few options instead of pinning it to one. That's what people drift toward — you leave space for what they haven't said yet, and it doesn't seem to strain you.

You also know how to move when you can't see the whole way. Today the options are spreading you thin, though. Choose one and keep it in front of you long enough to see what it actually is. The rest can stay in your hands; they don't have to be settled before you set them down. What's left is yours, and it can wait.

cells.tense: You are bracing for where all this feeling has to end up, and you're ahead of it.
cells.ask: Before you decide anything, write down what you actually feel about one situation and nothing about where it's headed — then leave the page alone for a day.
cells.core:
You reach for every feeling at once, so nothing has to surprise you. Ahead of the moment, you've already felt how each possibility would land and how it would go wrong — you arrive at people pre-felt. From the outside it looks like warmth. From inside it's a lot of holding.

And it is a lot: you're living in endings that haven't happened, and the person in front of you gets compared to a version you already rehearsed. One situation, one page: what you feel right now, not what it will mean. Then close the notebook and let the day stay open. Some of what you're bracing against may not arrive at all.

cells.tense: The possibilities were there once and you stopped reaching for them.
cells.ask: Tell one person one thing you feel about a situation you're in the middle of — no plan, no answer needed, no fixing it after.
cells.core:
You know how to leave room for the unnamed thing in someone. You've done it before. Lately you answer to the plainest reading and move on, and afterward you can't quite remember what the room felt like. Nothing is wrong with the plain reading. It's just the only one that comes now.

Small exchanges don't happen as much as they used to, so you skip them. It's a working arrangement, and it has kept you steady. But more feeling at once isn't available today. What is: one honest sentence to one person, and hearing what comes back without organizing it. That's enough to open the door a crack, and a crack is enough for now.

cells.tense: You are already tuning to what each person might feel, and calling it reading the room.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that you arranged something because of how someone might feel — then let the arranging be yours.
cells.core:
You pick up the room before anyone speaks. You pace the sentence, leave the pause, choose the softer word — and the evening lands the way you felt it would. That sensitivity does real work. You've just filed it under attention, under manners, under being good with people. Same act, no owner.

It isn't a small thing you do; it's the thing that decides how the room goes. Noticing it is not a boast. Say the plain fact to yourself or to someone: the choice was made because you could feel where it would land. That's your hand on it. Nobody else has to know the shape underneath.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has been gathering possibilities long, or that anything in their history made them careful or slow — so the Too Little cell may not locate a room behind them or name a cost, only say that the reaches aren't being made now. A reader could fairly say the many possibilities aren't intoxicating at all but just noise, so every cell keeps the abundance as theirs and the bend as the strain, not a verdict on the situation. The ask survives a wrong read because it's small, single, and finishable whether or not the diagnosis fits. The sentence that serves the writer more than them is the one about 'so many doors' — cut it; no poster line, no image of doors.
